The Romantic Poets & Idealised Love

The Romantic period (roughly 1785–1830) transformed how poets wrote about love. Instead of treating love as a rational arrangement, Romantic poets presented it as an overwhelming, often dangerous, emotional force. Three poems in the Relationships collection — Keats’s “La Belle Dame Sans Merci,” Byron’s “She Walks in Beauty” and Barrett Browning’s “Sonnet 43” — each offer a different vision of idealised love, and understanding how they compare is essential for the Part 1 comparison question.

La Belle Dame Sans Merci — John Keats (1819)

Keats (1795–1821) died of tuberculosis at just 25. His short life shaped his preoccupation with beauty, mortality and the pain of desire. “La Belle Dame Sans Merci” (“The Beautiful Lady Without Mercy”) tells the story of a knight who meets a mysterious, supernatural woman. She enchants him with “wild eyes,” feeds him exotic foods and lulls him to sleep — but he wakes alone on a cold hillside, “palely loitering.”

Key Fact

“La Belle Dame Sans Merci” presents love as a beautiful trap. The knight is seduced, enchanted and ultimately destroyed — Keats suggests that the more intensely we pursue beauty and love, the more devastating the loss when they vanish.

Key language: “I met a lady in the meads, / Full beautiful — a faery’s child” — the word “faery’s” immediately marks her as supernatural and otherworldly. She is not a real woman but an idealised fantasy. The ballad form (quatrains with an ABCB rhyme scheme) gives the poem a folk-tale quality, as if the knight’s suffering is part of an ancient, repeating pattern of men destroyed by desire.

Key structure: The poem uses a cyclical structure — it begins and ends on the “cold hill side” with “no birds sing.” This circularity traps the knight in his loss, suggesting he can never escape the memory of the beautiful lady. The barren landscape mirrors his emotional devastation.

In his dream, the knight sees “pale kings and princes too, / Pale warriors, death-pale were they all.” The repetition of “pale” creates a ghostly, death-like image — these are all previous victims of the belle dame. The listing of “kings,” “princes” and “warriors” suggests that no amount of power or status can protect a man from the destructive force of desire. They cry “La Belle Dame sans Merci / Thee hath in thrall!” — the knight is enslaved, just as they were.

She Walks in Beauty — Lord Byron (1814)

Byron (1788–1824) wrote this poem after seeing his cousin Anne Wilmot at a party, wearing a black mourning dress with spangles. The poem celebrates a woman’s beauty by comparing it to the balance between darkness and light in a starry night sky. Unlike Keats’s dangerous beauty, Byron’s subject is presented as perfectly harmonious.

Key language: “She walks in beauty, like the night / Of cloudless climes and starry skies” — the opening simile is unusual because beauty is typically compared to daylight, not darkness. Byron subverts this convention, presenting beauty as something mysterious, soft and restrained rather than dazzling. The alliteration of “cloudless climes” creates a smooth, flowing sound that mirrors the effortless elegance Byron describes.

Key structure: The poem has three regular six-line stanzas with an ABABAB rhyme scheme and iambic tetrameter (four stressed beats per line). This highly regular rhythm reflects the “perfect” balance Byron sees in the woman — nothing is excessive or out of place. The poem moves from external beauty (stanza 1) to inner goodness (stanza 3: “A mind at peace with all below, / A heart whose love is innocent”), suggesting that true beauty is both physical and moral.

Key Fact

Byron’s poem celebrates beauty without ever mentioning love, desire or possession. The speaker admires from a distance, never claiming the woman for himself. This restraint contrasts sharply with the consuming desire in Keats and the passionate devotion in Barrett Browning.

Sonnet 43: “How Do I Love Thee?” — Elizabeth Barrett Browning (1850)

Barrett Browning (1806–1861) wrote this as part of Sonnets from the Portuguese, a sequence of love poems to her husband Robert Browning. Their relationship was remarkable: Elizabeth was an invalid, six years older, and her controlling father forbade all his children from marrying. The couple eloped to Italy in 1846, and Elizabeth never saw her father again. The intensity of these poems reflects the depth of feeling in a relationship that was hard-won.

Key language: “How do I love thee? Let me count the ways” — the opening is a rhetorical question followed by a determined attempt to quantify something unquantifiable. The metaphor of “counting” love like a measurable quantity creates tension — Barrett Browning tries to express infinite feeling within the finite structure of a sonnet. The repetition of “I love thee” (eight times) builds like a chant or prayer, intensifying with each line.

Barrett Browning uses the Petrarchan sonnet form — 14 lines divided into an octave and sestet, with an ABBA ABBA CDC DCD rhyme scheme. This is the oldest and most traditional form for love poetry, stretching back to 14th-century Italy. By choosing this form, Barrett Browning places herself in a centuries-long tradition of poets trying to capture love in verse. But she transforms it: historically, Petrarchan sonnets were written by men about distant, unattainable women. Barrett Browning writes as a woman expressing her own desire — she is both the poet and the lover, which was radical for 1850.

Key structure: The poem builds from the everyday (“to the level of every day’s / Most quiet need”) to the transcendent (“I love thee with the breath, / Smiles, tears, of all my life; and, if God choose, / I shall but love thee better after death”). This escalation mirrors the overwhelming nature of love — it starts simply but ultimately surpasses even death. The final reference to loving “after death” gives the poem a spiritual, almost religious quality.

Comparing the Three Poems

Idealised love — three versions: Keats presents love as dangerous and destructive (the knight is left “alone and palely loitering”). Byron presents beauty as something to be admired from a distance, perfectly balanced but untouched. Barrett Browning presents love as a total, overwhelming commitment that transcends even death. All three idealise their subject, but the consequences are very different: destruction (Keats), reverence (Byron), and devotion (Barrett Browning).

Context links: All three poets write during or in the tradition of Romanticism, which valued intense personal emotion over rational restraint. However, Barrett Browning’s position as a female poet reshaping a male-dominated form (the sonnet) adds a layer of gender politics absent from Keats and Byron.

Family Love in the Relationships Collection

Not all poems in the collection are about romantic love. Three poems explore the intense, complicated bonds between parents and children: Joanna Baillie’s “A Child to his Sick Grandfather,” Vernon Scannell’s “Nettles” and Ingrid de Kok’s “My Father Would Not Show Us.” Each presents a different angle on parental protection — a child trying to protect a dying grandparent, a father protecting his child from physical pain, and a father failing to show his children vulnerability. These poems offer strong comparison material for the Part 1 question because they share the theme of family love but use very different methods.

A Child to his Sick Grandfather — Joanna Baillie (1790)

Baillie (1762–1851) was a Scottish poet and playwright who was widely admired in her lifetime but is now less well-known. This poem is spoken in the voice of a young child addressing a grandfather who is visibly ill and ageing. The child’s innocent, affectionate observations make the poem both tender and heartbreaking, because the reader understands what the child does not — the grandfather is dying.

Key Fact

The poem’s power comes from dramatic irony. The child cheerfully tries to comfort the grandfather (“you shall have my chair”), not understanding that no chair or kindness can reverse what is happening. The gap between the child’s innocent optimism and the reader’s knowledge of death creates deep pathos.

Key language: “Grand-dad, they say you’re old and frail, / Your stocked legs begin to fail” — the child catalogues the grandfather’s physical deterioration with innocent directness. There is no euphemism, no polite avoidance — the child describes what they see. The simple, monosyllabic vocabulary reflects the child’s young age and limited understanding, while the listing of failing body parts (head, leg, leg) creates a painful accumulation of decline.

Key structure: The poem is written in rhyming couplets with a regular rhythm, giving it a sing-song, nursery-rhyme quality that suits the child speaker. This innocently cheerful form contrasts with the devastating subject matter — the juxtaposition between the light form and the dark content is what makes the poem so moving.

Nettles — Vernon Scannell (1962)

Scannell (1922–2007) served in World War II and was deeply affected by his military experience. “Nettles” describes a simple incident: his young son falls into a bed of nettles and is stung. The father comforts the boy, then attacks the nettles with a billhook, but two weeks later they have regrown “tall as soldiers.” The poem is about a father’s desperate, futile desire to protect his child from pain.

Scannell uses a semantic field of war throughout: the nettles are a “regiment of spite,” “fallen dead,” and they later stand “tall as soldiers.” The father uses a “billhook” (a weapon-like tool) and makes a “funeral pyre” of the cut nettles. This military language transforms a domestic scene into a battle, reflecting Scannell’s war experience. The father fights the nettles like an enemy — but this enemy always returns, just as the threats to a child can never be permanently defeated.

Key structure: The poem is a single stanza of 16 lines in blank verse (iambic pentameter with some variation). The single stanza reflects the father’s single-minded determination to protect his son. The final two lines — “My son would often feel sharp wounds again. / Soothing him into a survey of his injuries” — shift the tone from triumph to resignation: the father knows he cannot always be there.

Key Fact

The final line — “My son would often feel sharp wounds again” — is the poem’s emotional heart. The father realises that no matter how fiercely he fights, he cannot protect his child from every pain life will bring. The nettles are a metaphor for all the hurts a parent cannot prevent.

My Father Would Not Show Us — Ingrid de Kok (1988)

De Kok (born 1951) is a South African poet. This poem describes a father who refuses to show his children his emotional or physical vulnerability. The title itself is a statement of absence — the father “would not show us” — and the poem explores what happens when a parent withholds the truth from their children out of a misguided desire to protect them.

Key language: The poem’s most striking feature is its use of negatives: “would not show us,” “would not let us see.” These repeated refusals create a sense of frustration and distance. The father’s silence is itself a form of protection — he believes hiding his pain shields his children — but it also creates a barrier between them. De Kok suggests that over-protection can become a form of emotional absence.

The father’s body becomes a map of concealed suffering. De Kok describes physical details — the father’s body, his hands, his illness — that the children are not allowed to see or discuss. This connects to ideas about masculinity and stoicism: the father has been taught that showing pain is weakness. The poem critiques this view, suggesting that by hiding his suffering, the father denies his children the chance to comfort him — reversing the usual parent-child dynamic.

Key structure: The poem uses free verse with irregular line lengths, reflecting the halting, uncertain way the speaker remembers and tries to understand the father’s behaviour. There is no comforting rhyme or rhythm — the form mirrors the emotional discomfort of a relationship defined by what was hidden rather than what was shared.

Comparing the Three Poems

Protection as a theme: Baillie’s child tries to protect the grandfather through innocent kindness. Scannell’s father tries to protect his son through physical action (destroying the nettles). De Kok’s father tries to protect his children by hiding his vulnerability. All three attempts fail — the grandfather will die, the nettles will regrow, and the father’s silence creates distance rather than safety.

Form reflects emotion: Baillie’s rhyming couplets create innocent simplicity; Scannell’s blank verse creates determined, measured control; de Kok’s free verse creates uncertainty and emotional fragmentation. In the exam, comparing how form supports meaning across these poems is a strong way to demonstrate AO2 skills.

When Love Fails

Romantic love does not always last. Three poems in the Relationships collection examine what happens when love fades, fails or becomes something unrecognisable: Wordsworth’s “A Complaint,” Hardy’s “Neutral Tones” and Jennings’s “One Flesh.” Each poet presents disillusionment differently — through loss of emotional connection, through bitter memory, and through the quiet erosion of a marriage — but all three convey the pain of love that no longer sustains.

A Complaint — William Wordsworth (1807)

Wordsworth (1770–1850) is one of the founders of English Romanticism. “A Complaint” is believed to address his friend Samuel Taylor Coleridge, whose emotional withdrawal and opium addiction had strained their friendship. The poem mourns the loss of a deep emotional bond — not a romantic relationship, but a platonic love that was once sustaining and is now reduced to almost nothing.

Key Fact

Wordsworth uses an extended metaphor of a fountain to describe the relationship. It was once “a fountain at my fond heart’s door” that “never ceased to flow” — constant, generous, life-giving. Now it has been replaced by “A well of love — it may be deep — / I trust it is, — and never dry” — a well that may still exist but is hidden, inaccessible and uncertain. The shift from fountain (visible, overflowing) to well (underground, stagnant) captures the devastating change.

Key language: The dashes in “it may be deep — / I trust it is, — and never dry” create hesitation and doubt. The speaker is trying to convince himself that the love still exists, but the broken syntax reveals his uncertainty. The word “trust” is loaded — trust is precisely what has been damaged.

Key structure: The poem has three stanzas: past (the fountain), present (the well), and reflection. This chronological movement from abundance to scarcity mirrors the deterioration of the relationship. The regular metre and rhyme scheme create a controlled, measured tone that contrasts with the emotional pain beneath — Wordsworth keeps his composure even as he mourns.

Neutral Tones — Thomas Hardy (1867)

Hardy (1840–1928) wrote this poem at 27, drawing on a painful romantic experience. It describes a moment when two lovers stand by a pond, recognising that their love is dead. The poem is a memory, recalled years later, and the bitter, stripped-back imagery reflects the speaker’s enduring pain.

Key language: “We stood by a pond that winter day, / And the sun was white, as though chidden of God” — the pathetic fallacy is immediately established. The sun is not warm or golden but “white” and punished (“chidden”), drained of all vitality. The pond, the leaves, the sky — everything in the landscape is bleached and lifeless, reflecting the death of feeling between the lovers.

The simile comparing the lover’s gaze to someone looking at “tedious riddles” is devastating. The word “tedious” suggests boredom and irritation — the speaker has become a puzzle the lover no longer cares to solve. “Rove” implies the eyes wander without focus, suggesting the lover is mentally absent. The speaker is right there, but emotionally the lover has already left.

Key structure: Like Keats’s “La Belle Dame Sans Merci,” Hardy uses a cyclical structure. The poem begins and ends at the pond, with the final stanza: “And a pond edged with greyish leaves.” This return traps the speaker in the memory — he cannot escape the moment when he realised love had died. The four regular quatrains with an ABAB rhyme scheme create a deceptively orderly surface that barely contains the bitterness beneath.

Key Fact

The title “Neutral Tones” is deeply ironic. There is nothing neutral about the poem — it is suffused with bitterness and pain. The “neutral” refers to the drained, colourless landscape and the empty feelings between the lovers, but the speaker’s enduring memory of this moment, decades later, proves that the emotions were anything but neutral.

One Flesh — Elizabeth Jennings (1966)

Jennings (1926–2001) was the only female member of “The Movement,” a group of 1950s English poets who rejected Romantic excess in favour of clarity, restraint and understatement. “One Flesh” describes her elderly parents lying apart in bed, their marriage intact in name but emotionally distant. The title alludes to the Biblical phrase from Genesis 2:24 (“and they shall be one flesh”) — though Jennings’ poem inverts the ideal, showing a couple who are physically apart rather than united.

Key language: “Lying apart now, each in a separate bed, / He with a survey, she with a book” — the opening is deliberately mundane. The couple is separated physically (different beds) and mentally (different activities). Yet the word “now” implies this was not always the case — the distance has grown over time. “Tossed up like flotsam from a former passion” is a powerful simile: flotsam is wreckage left after a storm, suggesting their current state is the remnant of a love that once had the force of a tempest.

This paradox captures the central mystery of long marriages. The couple are physically and emotionally distant (“apart”), yet bound by decades of shared history (“close together”). The repetition of “strangely” suggests that even the speaker — their own child — cannot fully understand the nature of this bond. It is neither love nor not-love, neither together nor separate. Jennings presents long-term relationships as irreducibly complex.

Key structure: Three regular six-line stanzas with a quiet, understated tone. The regularity of the form mirrors the routine of the couple’s life — predictable, orderly, but lacking passion. The final stanza shifts from observation to reflection: “Whose fire from which I came, has now grown cold?” This question acknowledges that the speaker’s own existence was the product of passion that no longer exists — a deeply unsettling realisation.

Comparing the Three Poems

Different stages of love’s decline: Wordsworth mourns a love that has recently withdrawn (the fountain has just become a well). Hardy bitterly remembers the exact moment love died (by the pond). Jennings observes the long aftermath of love’s slow erosion (her parents in old age). Together, they trace a full arc: loss, death, and the long, quiet aftermath.

Tone contrast: Wordsworth is measured and controlled; Hardy is bitter and ironic; Jennings is contemplative and sad. These tonal differences reflect different relationships with disappointment — Wordsworth still hopes, Hardy has given up, Jennings simply observes with quiet puzzlement.

before.content_html:
Power, Control & Unconventional Love

Love and power are closely linked in the Relationships collection. Three poems explore what happens when love involves control, violence or a refusal to be conventional: Robert Browning’s “My Last Duchess,” Carol Ann Duffy’s “Valentine” and Simon Armitage’s “The Manhunt.” Each poem challenges the reader to think about who holds power in a relationship and how love can be distorted by possession, honesty or trauma.

My Last Duchess — Robert Browning (1842)

Browning (1812–1889) based this poem on a real historical figure: Alfonso II, Duke of Ferrara, whose first wife Lucrezia de’ Medici died aged 17 under suspicious circumstances. The Duke is speaking to an envoy sent to negotiate his next marriage. As he shows off a portrait of his dead wife, he reveals — without meaning to — that he had her killed because she was too easily pleased by other people and things.

Key Fact

The poem is a dramatic monologue. The Duke believes he is demonstrating his power and good taste, but the reader sees a controlling, jealous man who murdered his wife because he could not tolerate her independent spirit. The gap between the Duke’s self-image and the reader’s perception is the poem’s central irony.

Key language: “That’s my last Duchess painted on the wall, / Looking as if she were alive” — the possessive pronoun “my” in the opening line immediately establishes ownership. The Duchess is “my last” — an object in a collection, with the chilling implication that there will be a next. “Looking as if she were alive” is casually menacing: the reader wonders why she is no longer alive and quickly learns the answer.

“I gave commands; / Then all smiles stopped together” — this is the poem’s most terrifying moment. The euphemism “gave commands” barely conceals what it means: he ordered her death. The abruptness of “all smiles stopped” mirrors the sudden, final nature of the act. The Duke recounts murder with the same composure he uses to discuss art — the casualness is horrifying.

The poem is written in heroic couplets (rhyming pairs of iambic pentameter lines), but the enjambment frequently disguises the rhymes, making the speech sound natural and conversational. This reflects the Duke’s smooth, controlled manner — he is performing civility while revealing monstrous truths. The single continuous stanza, with no breaks, mirrors the Duke’s refusal to allow interruption: he controls the conversation just as he controlled the Duchess.

Valentine — Carol Ann Duffy (1993)

Duffy (born 1955) was the UK’s first female and first openly LGBTQ+ Poet Laureate. “Valentine” rejects commercial Valentine’s Day clichés (“Not a red rose or a satin heart”) and instead offers an onion as a gift of love. The onion becomes an extended metaphor for the many layers of a real relationship — including the parts that make you cry.

Key language: “It will blind you with tears / like a lover” — the onion makes you cry, just as real love does. The verb “blind” suggests love can be overwhelming, obscuring clear judgment. “Its fierce kiss will stay on your lips” presents love as intense and lingering, with the adjective “fierce” hinting at aggression as well as passion. As the poem progresses, the tone darkens: “Its scent will cling to your fingers, / cling to your knife” — the final word, “knife,” introduces violence and danger, suggesting that love can wound as well as nourish.

Key Fact

The poem moves from playful to possessive. The opening is witty and charming (“I give you an onion”), but by the end, words like “possessive,” “faithful” and “cling to your knife” suggest love can become controlling and even dangerous. Duffy refuses to pretend love is only positive — her honesty is the poem’s greatest strength.

Key structure: The poem uses free verse with irregular stanza lengths, reflecting the speaker’s rejection of conventional romance. Short, single-line stanzas (“Not a red rose or a satin heart”; “I give you an onion”; “Take it”) interrupt the flow like commands, becoming increasingly insistent. The final one-word line — “Lethal” (in some editions) or the knife image — ends the poem on a sharp, threatening note.

The Manhunt — Simon Armitage (2007)

Armitage (born 1963) wrote this poem after interviewing Laura, the wife of Eddie Beddoes, a soldier who served in Bosnia and returned with severe PTSD and a bullet lodged near his spine. The poem is written from Laura’s perspective as she carefully, tenderly tries to map her husband’s damaged body and mind. The title “The Manhunt” refers to her search for the man her husband used to be.

Key language: “And handle and hold / the damaged, porcelain collar-bone” — the juxtaposition of “damaged” and “porcelain” captures the soldier’s condition: porcelain is beautiful but fragile, suggesting the body is both precious and breakable. “Handle and hold” uses gentle, careful verbs — Laura treats her husband like something that might shatter. The poem is full of sensory imagery focused on touch, reflecting the intimate, physical process of reconnection.

The “frozen river” is a metaphor for a scar on the soldier’s face. “Frozen” implies the wound has stopped healing emotionally — it is permanent, fixed, cold. “Trace” is an intimate verb: Laura follows the scar with her finger, trying to read the map of his suffering. The phrase “Only then would he let me” establishes the poem’s key dynamic — the soldier controls access to his body and emotions, gradually allowing Laura closer. The enjambment between “trace” and “the frozen river” mirrors this slow, careful process of unfolding.

Key structure: The poem consists of rhyming or near-rhyming couplets that gradually move from the soldier’s external wounds (collar-bone, jaw, chest) to his internal trauma (a “foetus of metal” — the bullet — and his “unexploded mine” of emotional pain). This inward journey mirrors Laura’s search: she starts with what she can see and touch, and slowly reaches the hidden psychological damage that is harder to heal.

Comparing the Three Poems

Who holds power? Browning’s Duke holds absolute power — he controls the Duchess in life and death, and now controls her image. Duffy’s speaker starts as a playful gift-giver but becomes increasingly possessive (“Lethal”). Armitage’s soldier holds the power of access — Laura can only explore as far as he allows. Power operates differently in each relationship: through murder, through language, and through emotional withdrawal.

Unconventional love: None of these poems presents a conventional, happy love story. Browning shows love corrupted by possession. Duffy shows love as honest but potentially dangerous. Armitage shows love as a patient, painful process of reconnection after trauma. Together, they argue that real relationships are far more complex than the “red roses and satin hearts” Duffy rejects.

before.content_html:
Modern Love & Everyday Voices

Not all love poetry is serious or tragic. Three contemporary poems in the Relationships collection use humour, pop culture and everyday language to explore love in ways that feel immediate and accessible: Wendy Cope’s paired poems “1st Date — She” and “1st Date — He,” John Cooper Clarke’s “i wanna be yours” and Jen Hatfield’s “Love’s Dog.” These poems offer a refreshing contrast to the Romantic and literary heritage poems in the collection, and they are excellent choices for comparison because their modern methods stand out against older traditions.

1st Date — She & 1st Date — He — Wendy Cope (2011)

Cope (born 1945) is known for witty, accessible poetry that often satirises literary conventions. These paired poems give both sides of a first date: “She” presents the woman’s nervous inner monologue, “He” presents the man’s. Cope treats them as a single poem (they are listed together in the anthology), and the humour comes from recognising the universal anxiety and self-consciousness of meeting someone new.

Key Fact

The poem’s dual perspective structure is its most distinctive feature. By placing “She” and “He” side by side, Cope reveals both the similarities (both are nervous, both want to impress) and the differences (gendered anxieties about appearance, conversation, physical attraction) between men and women approaching the same moment.

Key language: Both speakers use a colloquial register — the inner monologue sounds like real thought, not crafted poetry. “She” worries about whether her outfit works, whether she’s talking too much, whether he’ll call again. “He” worries about whether she finds him attractive, whether he’s being funny enough. The conversational tone makes both speakers endearing and relatable — the reader recognises their own nervousness.

Key structure: Both poems use short lines, simple vocabulary and a loose structure that mimics the jumpy, fragmented quality of anxious thought. The lack of a regular rhyme scheme or metre reflects the unpredictability of a first date — neither speaker knows what will happen next. The paired format (two poems read together) is structurally unique in the anthology and invites comparison in itself.

i wanna be yours — John Cooper Clarke (1982)

Cooper Clarke (born 1949) is a “punk poet” from Salford, Greater Manchester, who performed his poetry alongside punk bands in the late 1970s. “i wanna be yours” was written to be spoken aloud, not read silently on a page. The poem was set to music by the Arctic Monkeys in 2013, introducing it to a new generation. The title’s deliberate lack of capitalisation and use of “wanna” signals its anti-establishment attitude from the start.

Cooper Clarke replaces traditional poetic imagery (roses, stars, moonlight) with deliberately mundane domestic objects: “I wanna be your vacuum cleaner / breathing in your dust.” He offers to be a Ford Cortina, a raincoat, an electric heater, a coffee pot. These objects are functional, unglamorous and everyday — the opposite of Romantic idealism. Yet this is precisely the point: the speaker is not offering grand gestures but total, practical devotion. He wants to be useful, warm, reliable — to serve the beloved in the most ordinary ways possible. This makes the love feel more genuine than any sonnet’s declarations.

Key language: “I wanna be your electric meter / I will not run out” — the promise “I will not run out” is the poem’s emotional core, cutting through the humour with a sincere pledge of constancy. The anaphora of “I wanna be your” creates a hypnotic, chant-like rhythm suited to performance. The refrain “I wanna be yours” shifts from comic to genuinely moving through repetition — what starts as a joke becomes an earnest declaration.

Key structure: The poem has no punctuation and minimal capitalisation, reflecting its punk, anti-establishment origins and its performance roots. The regular stanza pattern and relentless anaphora give it a song-like quality — it was always meant to be heard, not just read. The deliberate rejection of “literary” language is itself a statement about who gets to write love poetry and in what voice.

Love’s Dog — Jen Hatfield (2012)

Hatfield (born 1978) is a Scottish poet who lived for several years on the Shetland Islands. “Love’s Dog” presents love as a contradictory, unpredictable companion — like a dog that can be both loyal and wild, comforting and maddening. The poem takes its title from the idea that love follows us around, sometimes wanted, sometimes not.

Key language: The poem is built around a series of oxymorons and contradictions: “What I love about love is its / What I hate about love is its.” Each stanza pairs something loved with something hated, presenting love as inherently dual — it cannot exist without its opposite. The parallel structure (“What I love… What I hate…”) creates a see-sawing rhythm that mirrors the emotional ups and downs of being in love.

Key Fact

Hatfield presents love as fundamentally paradoxical — you cannot have the joy without the pain, the excitement without the anxiety, the closeness without the vulnerability. The poem refuses to simplify love into either a positive or negative experience, making it one of the most honest and psychologically complex poems in the collection.

The title “Love’s Dog” is a metaphor in itself. A dog is loyal but unpredictable, affectionate but capable of biting, always following you whether you want it to or not. Love, Hatfield suggests, is the same — it is not something you can fully control. The alternating love/hate structure across the poem mirrors the unpredictable behaviour of a dog that might lick your face one moment and chew your shoes the next. The structural tension between the rigid parallel pattern and the wild, surprising content within each line embodies this perfectly: love has a pattern, but it constantly surprises you.

Comparing the Three Poems

Contemporary voices: All three poems reject the elevated diction and formal structures of the Romantic and literary heritage poems. Cope uses colloquial inner monologue, Cooper Clarke uses punk-influenced domestic imagery, and Hatfield uses philosophical paradox. Each finds a fresh way to write about love without relying on centuries-old conventions.

Humour and honesty: All three poems are funny, but the humour serves a serious purpose. Cope’s humour reveals the universal vulnerability of new love. Cooper Clarke’s humour disguises a sincere pledge of devotion. Hatfield’s humour highlights the contradictions of love. In each case, humour makes the emotional truth more convincing, not less.

before.content_html:
Why Form, Structure & Language Matter

In the Part 1 comparison question, form and structure are essential AO2 targets. The Relationships collection contains a wide range of poetic forms, and understanding why each poet chose a particular form — and how that form shapes meaning — is what separates a competent answer from a perceptive one. This lesson maps the key forms across all 15 poems so you can make informed choices in the exam.

Sonnets: Love’s Traditional Container

The sonnet is the most established form for love poetry, stretching back to 14th-century Italy. Two poems in the collection use it:

Barrett Browning’s “Sonnet 43” uses the Petrarchan form (ABBA ABBA CDC DCD). The octave poses the question (“How do I love thee?”) and the sestet answers it with escalating intensity. The traditional form is significant because Petrarchan sonnets were historically written by men about idealised women — Barrett Browning subverts this by writing as a woman declaring her own passionate love.

Hardy’s “Neutral Tones” uses a modified sonnet-like structure (four quatrains, 16 lines) that echoes but does not quite conform to the sonnet tradition. This near-miss mirrors the poem’s theme: something that was once whole (love) has become incomplete and broken.

Key Fact

When writing about sonnets, always explain the relationship between the form and the content. Barrett Browning uses the traditional love sonnet to declare her own desire (radical for a woman in 1850). Hardy uses a sonnet-like form for a poem about love’s death — subverting the form traditionally associated with love’s celebration.

Dramatic Monologue: The Unreliable Speaker

Browning’s “My Last Duchess” is a dramatic monologue in heroic couplets (rhyming pairs of iambic pentameter). The form creates a double layer of meaning: the Duke thinks he is presenting himself as cultured and powerful, but the reader sees a possessive murderer. The enjambment across the couplets disguises the rhyme, making the speech sound natural while maintaining poetic control — mirroring the Duke’s smooth exterior hiding a violent interior.

Keats’s “La Belle Dame Sans Merci” uses the ballad form: quatrains with an ABCB rhyme scheme and a shortened fourth line in each stanza. This gives the poem a folk-tale quality, as though the knight’s story has been told many times before. The shortened fourth line creates a halting, incomplete rhythm that mirrors the knight’s interrupted happiness. The ballad’s oral tradition also implies universality — this is not just one knight’s story but a pattern repeated throughout history.

Free Verse: Breaking the Rules

Several contemporary poems use free verse, which does not follow a fixed metre or rhyme scheme. In each case, the choice is deliberate:

Duffy’s “Valentine” uses free verse to mirror her rejection of conventional romance. Short, single-line stanzas (“Take it”) become commands that grow increasingly insistent. The irregularity reflects real emotion — messy, unpredictable, sometimes aggressive.

De Kok’s “My Father Would Not Show Us” uses free verse with irregular line lengths to reflect the halting uncertainty of trying to understand a parent’s emotional withdrawal.

Armitage’s “The Manhunt” uses loosely rhyming couplets in free verse — the near-rhymes suggest connection that is not quite achieved, mirroring Laura’s incomplete understanding of her husband’s trauma.

Key Language Techniques Across the Collection

Key Fact

The examiner rewards analysis of effect, not just identification. Naming a technique is worth one mark at most. Explaining how it creates meaning in context — and comparing how two poets use similar or different techniques to achieve different effects — is where the top marks lie.

Imagery patterns: Pathetic fallacy (Hardy: white sun, greyish leaves), sensory imagery (Armitage: touch-based metaphors), domestic imagery (Cooper Clarke: vacuum cleaners and electric heaters), natural imagery (Keats: cold hillside; Scannell: nettles as soldiers). These different semantic fields reflect each poet’s vision of love: natural, domestic, sensory or bleak.

Tone shifts: Many poems contain a volta or tonal shift. Duffy’s “Valentine” moves from playful to possessive. Jennings’s “One Flesh” moves from observation to a disturbing personal question. Armitage’s “The Manhunt” moves from external to internal. Identifying and analysing these shifts shows sophisticated structural awareness.

Regular forms (sonnets, rhyming couplets, ballads, consistent stanzas) suggest control, tradition, certainty or order. Barrett Browning’s sonnet channels emotion through a disciplined form; Byron’s ABABAB rhyme reflects the “perfect balance” of beauty. Irregular forms (free verse, mixed stanza lengths) suggest disruption, honesty, modernity or emotional complexity. Duffy’s free verse refuses the constraints of traditional romance; de Kok’s irregular lines reflect emotional fragmentation. When two poems use contrasting forms, this is itself a point of comparison for AO2.

Quick Reference: Form Map

Petrarchan sonnet: Sonnet 43 (Barrett Browning). Modified sonnet/quatrains: Neutral Tones (Hardy). Ballad: La Belle Dame Sans Merci (Keats). Dramatic monologue (heroic couplets): My Last Duchess (Browning). Regular stanzas, ABABAB: She Walks in Beauty (Byron). Rhyming couplets: A Child to his Sick Grandfather (Baillie). Free verse: Valentine (Duffy), My Father Would Not Show Us (de Kok), Love’s Dog (Hatfield). Loosely rhyming couplets: The Manhunt (Armitage), Nettles (Scannell). Performance/no punctuation: i wanna be yours (Cooper Clarke). Dual perspective: 1st Date — She / He (Cope). Regular stanzas: One Flesh (Jennings), A Complaint (Wordsworth).

before.content_html:
The Part 1 Comparison Question

Edexcel Component 2, Section B, Part 1 asks you to compare a named poem (printed in the exam paper) with one other poem of your choice from the same collection. The question is worth 20 marks: 15 for AO2 (language, form and structure) and 5 for AO3 (context). You are expected to write a sustained, comparative essay — not two separate analyses.

Key Fact

The named poem is printed on the exam paper, so you can quote directly from it. Your chosen poem is closed book — you must quote from memory. This means you need to memorise 4–5 short, versatile quotations from every poem you might choose. Practise writing them out from memory before the exam.

Step 1: Read the Question Carefully

The question will always follow the same pattern: “Compare how [poet] in [named poem] and one other poem from the Relationships collection present [theme/aspect].” The theme might be “love,” “loss,” “power,” “family,” “desire” or a more specific aspect. Your first job is to identify the focus of the question and choose a comparison poem that gives you plenty to say about that focus.

Choosing your poem: Pick a poem that has clear similarities and differences with the named poem on the given theme. If the named poem presents love as destructive (e.g. “La Belle Dame Sans Merci”), you could compare with “My Last Duchess” (love as possession) for a similarity-based comparison, or “Sonnet 43” (love as devotion) for a contrast-based comparison. Both approaches work — the key is that you can discuss method (AO2) in both poems.

Step 2: Plan Before You Write

Spend 5 minutes planning. A strong plan has 3–4 comparative points, each covering both poems:

Named poem: La Belle Dame Sans Merci (Keats). Chosen poem: Sonnet 43 (Barrett Browning).

Point 1 — Both present love as overwhelming: Keats: the knight is enchanted, enslaved (“in thrall”). Barrett Browning: the speaker is consumed (“I love thee to the depth and breadth and height / My soul can reach”). But Keats’s love destroys; Barrett Browning’s transcends death.

Point 2 — Form shapes meaning: Keats uses the ballad — folk-tale, cyclical, suggesting love’s destructive power is timeless. Barrett Browning uses the Petrarchan sonnet — traditional love form, subverted by a female voice. Both use established forms but to opposite ends: Keats shows love’s curse, Barrett Browning shows love’s blessing.

Point 3 — Context: Keats (TB, early death) sees beauty as fleeting and dangerous. Barrett Browning (elopement, defying her father) channels hard-won love into the sonnet tradition she was excluded from as a woman.

Step 3: Write Comparatively Throughout

The biggest mistake students make is writing about Poem A, then writing about Poem B, then bolting on a comparison at the end. This is called the “tennis match” approach and it limits your marks. Instead, use a comparative structure where every paragraph discusses both poems:

Key Fact

Use this paragraph structure: Point (what both poets do), Evidence from Poem A (quote + AO2 analysis), Link to Poem B (comparative connective), Evidence from Poem B (quote + AO2 analysis), AO3 context (for one or both poems). This ensures every paragraph is genuinely comparative.

Comparative connectives: Use these to link your analysis of both poems within each paragraph:

For similarities: “Similarly,” “Both poets…,” “In the same way,” “Like [poet A], [poet B] also…”

For differences: “In contrast,” “Whereas,” “However,” “While [poet A]…, [poet B]…,” “Unlike [poet A], [poet B]…”

For nuance: “Although both poets…, they differ in…,” “On the surface…, but on closer analysis…,” “This is complicated by…”

Step 4: Embed AO2 and AO3

AO2 (15 marks): This is where most marks are. You must analyse how poets create meaning through language (imagery, metaphor, word choice), form (sonnet, ballad, free verse, dramatic monologue) and structure (stanza patterns, volta, cyclical structure, progression). Always name the technique, quote, and explain the effect.

AO3 (5 marks): Context should be woven in, not bolted on. Instead of a separate context paragraph, integrate it into your analysis: “Barrett Browning’s use of the Petrarchan sonnet is particularly significant because this form was traditionally reserved for male poets praising distant, silent women; by writing as a woman declaring her own desire, she subverts a centuries-old convention.”

[Point] Both Keats and Barrett Browning present love as an overwhelming force that consumes the speaker entirely, yet the consequences of that overwhelming love are radically different. [Poem A + AO2] In “La Belle Dame Sans Merci,” Keats describes the knight as being held “in thrall” by the beautiful lady — the word “thrall” means slavery, suggesting love has imprisoned him. The cyclical ballad structure reinforces this: the poem begins and ends on the “cold hill side,” trapping the knight in a repeating cycle of enchantment and loss. [Link] In contrast, Barrett Browning presents overwhelming love as liberating rather than imprisoning. [Poem B + AO2] In “Sonnet 43,” the anaphora of “I love thee” builds through the octave like a rising tide, reaching its climax in “I shall but love thee better after death” — love here transcends even mortality. [AO3] Barrett Browning’s confident declaration is all the more striking given that she wrote this as a woman in 1850, subverting the Petrarchan sonnet tradition in which women were silent objects of male admiration.

Common Mistakes to Avoid

1. Writing two separate essays: Every paragraph must discuss both poems. 2. Retelling the poem: The examiner knows the poems — analyse, don’t summarise. 3. Spotting techniques without explaining their effect: “Keats uses alliteration” earns almost nothing. “Keats’s alliteration in ‘cold hill side’ creates a hard, bitter sound that…” earns marks. 4. Forgetting AO3: Context is worth 5 marks — a quarter of the total. 5. Choosing a weak comparison poem: Pick one you know well and that offers clear points of comparison. Don’t choose a poem just because you know quotes from it.

before.content_html:
Exam Day Preparation

This final lesson brings together everything you have learned across the collection. Your anthology comparison question will test your ability to select, compare and analyse two poems under timed conditions. The challenge is not just knowledge — it is making fast, confident decisions about which poem to choose and what to write about. This lesson gives you the tools to do that: a decision-making framework, a complete quotation bank for all 15 poems, and strategies for writing under pressure.

The Question Format

Anthology comparison questions typically follow a similar pattern: you are asked to compare how poets present a given theme or aspect of relationships in a named poem and one other poem from your studied collection. The named poem is usually printed in full on the question paper. You choose the second poem from memory. You are assessed on AO2 (language, form and structure) and AO3 (context). Check your exam board’s specimen paper for the exact wording, mark allocations and recommended timings.

Key Fact

You do not need to prepare all 15 poems equally. Choose 4–5 poems that you know deeply — these become your “go-to” choices for any question. A well-analysed poem you know thoroughly will always outscore a poem you half-remember. Quality of analysis beats breadth of knowledge.

Choosing Your Comparison Poem: A Decision Framework

When you see the named poem and the theme, ask yourself three questions:

1. Which of my prepared poems connects to this theme? If the theme is “loss,” your options include “Neutral Tones,” “A Complaint,” “One Flesh,” “La Belle Dame Sans Merci.” If it is “power,” consider “My Last Duchess,” “Valentine,” “The Manhunt.”

2. Can I identify both similarities AND differences? The best comparisons have both. A poem that is simply “the same” as the named poem gives you less to say than one with interesting contrasts in method, tone or context.

3. Can I discuss form and structure, not just language? If your only point is about imagery, you are missing AO2 marks. Choose a poem where you can compare form (sonnet vs free verse), structure (cyclical vs linear) or voice (dramatic monologue vs first person).

Idealised / passionate love: Sonnet 43 + She Walks in Beauty + La Belle Dame Sans Merci + i wanna be yours

Love gone wrong / loss: Neutral Tones + A Complaint + One Flesh + La Belle Dame Sans Merci

Power and control: My Last Duchess + Valentine + The Manhunt

Family / protection: A Child to his Sick Grandfather + Nettles + My Father Would Not Show Us

Modern / everyday love: 1st Date She/He + i wanna be yours + Love’s Dog + Valentine

Distance / emotional barriers: A Complaint + One Flesh + The Manhunt + My Father Would Not Show Us + Neutral Tones

Quotation Bank: All 15 Poems

Below are 3–4 key quotations per poem. For your chosen “go-to” poems, memorise all of these. For the others, know at least one. Each quotation is paired with its main analytical focus.

La Belle Dame Sans Merci (Keats):

• “Full beautiful — a faery’s child” — supernatural, idealised beauty (AO2: imagery). • “La Belle Dame sans Merci / Thee hath in thrall” — love as enslavement (AO2: metaphor). • “Alone and palely loitering” — devastation after love’s loss (AO2: pathetic fallacy). • “And no birds sing” — cyclical refrain, nature emptied (AO2: structure).

A Child to his Sick Grandfather (Baillie):

• “Grand-dad, they say you’re old and frail” — innocent directness cataloguing decline (AO2: voice). • “I’ll lead you kindly by the hand” — child’s tender, inadequate comfort (AO2: voice). • Rhyming couplets — nursery-rhyme quality contrasts with death (AO2: form).

She Walks in Beauty (Byron):

• “She walks in beauty, like the night / Of cloudless climes and starry skies” — beauty compared to darkness (AO2: simile). • “One shade the more, one ray the less” — perfect balance (AO2: antithesis). • “A mind at peace with all below, / A heart whose love is innocent” — inner beauty (AO2: structure — external to internal).

A Complaint (Wordsworth):

• “A fountain at my fond heart’s door” — love as visible abundance (AO2: extended metaphor). • “A well of love — it may be deep” — dashes create doubt (AO2: punctuation). • Three-stanza structure: past, present, reflection (AO2: structure).

Neutral Tones (Hardy):

• “The sun was white, as though chidden of God” — drained, punished landscape (AO2: pathetic fallacy). • “Your eyes on me were as eyes that rove / Over tedious riddles” — boredom and indifference (AO2: simile). • “And a pond edged with greyish leaves” — cyclical return to the scene (AO2: structure).

My Last Duchess (Browning):

• “That’s my last Duchess painted on the wall” — possessive pronoun, ownership (AO2: word choice). • “I gave commands; / Then all smiles stopped together” — euphemism for murder (AO2: understatement). • “Looking as if she were alive” — casually menacing (AO2: dramatic irony). • Single-stanza dramatic monologue (AO2: form).

Sonnet 43 (Barrett Browning):

• “How do I love thee? Let me count the ways” — quantifying the unquantifiable (AO2: rhetorical question). • “I love thee to the depth and breadth and height / My soul can reach” — spatial metaphor for limitless love (AO2: imagery). • “I shall but love thee better after death” — love transcending mortality (AO2: volta). • Petrarchan sonnet form — female poet subverting male tradition (AO3: context).

1st Date She/He (Cope): • Dual perspective — both sides of dating anxiety (AO2: structure). • Colloquial inner monologue (AO2: voice).

Valentine (Duffy): • “Not a red rose or a satin heart” — rejecting clichés (AO2: opening). • “It will blind you with tears” — love causes pain (AO2: metaphor). • “Its scent will cling to your fingers, / cling to your knife” — darkening to violence (AO2: tone shift).

One Flesh (Jennings): • “Lying apart now, each in a separate bed” — physical and emotional distance (AO2: imagery). • “Tossed up like flotsam from a former passion” — wreckage of love (AO2: simile). • “Strangely apart, yet strangely close together” — paradox (AO2: language). • “Whose fire from which I came, has now grown cold?” — unsettling final question (AO2: volta).

i wanna be yours (Cooper Clarke): • “I wanna be your vacuum cleaner / breathing in your dust” — domestic devotion (AO2: metaphor). • “I will not run out” — sincere constancy (AO2: tone shift). • Anaphora of “I wanna be your” — hypnotic repetition (AO2: structure).

Love’s Dog (Hatfield): • “What I love about love is its / What I hate about love is its” — love as paradox (AO2: structure). • Oxymorons throughout (AO2: language).

Nettles (Scannell): • “A regiment of spite” — military semantic field (AO2: imagery). • “Tall as soldiers” — nettles regrow, protection is futile (AO2: metaphor). • Single stanza, blank verse (AO2: form).

The Manhunt (Armitage): • “The damaged, porcelain collar-bone” — fragile beauty (AO2: juxtaposition). • “The frozen river which ran through his face” — scar as landscape (AO2: metaphor). • “Only then would he let me” — gradual access (AO2: structure). • Inward journey: external wounds to hidden PTSD (AO2: structure).

My Father Would Not Show Us (de Kok): • “Would not show us,” “would not let us see” — repeated negatives (AO2: language). • Free verse with irregular lines (AO2: form). • The body as concealed text (AO2: imagery).

Key Fact

The strongest students walk into the exam with 3–4 pre-planned comparison pairings. For example: “If they ask about loss, I’ll compare with Neutral Tones. If they ask about power, I’ll compare with My Last Duchess. If they ask about family, I’ll compare with Nettles.” Adapt these to the specific question wording, but having a starting point saves valuable planning time.

Writing Under Pressure: Final Checklist

Before writing: Read the question twice. Identify the theme. Choose your poem. Plan 3 points (each covering both poems). While writing: Start every paragraph with a comparative point. Quote from both poems (the named poem from the paper, your chosen poem from memory). Analyse how (AO2), not just what. Weave in context (AO3). After writing: Check you have discussed both poems in every paragraph. Check you have mentioned form or structure at least once. Check for spelling and punctuation.
